topic: The Origin and Color Dependence of the Index of Refraction

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Lorentz Oscillator Model
sections.content: Briefly introduce electrons in a material as 'bound' to the nucleus by a spring-like force. When an electromagnetic wave (light) strikes, the electron oscillates, creating a secondary dipole field. The phase difference between the driving wave and the electron's response determines the refractive index.
sections.example: Visualize an electron as a mass on a spring; light is the rhythmic shaking of the support base.

sections.title: The Origin of Refractive Index (n)
sections.content: Explain that the index of refraction n = c/v. Since the electron's dipole radiation interferes with the original light wave, the resulting 'effective' wave travels slower. Mathematically, n is related to the polarizability of the medium (n² ≈ 1 + χ).
sections.example: A hiker (light) walking through a dense forest (medium) with many 'bouncy' obstacles (electrons) that cause the hiker to adjust speed.

sections.title: Color Dependence (Dispersion)
sections.content: Introduce the resonance frequency (ω₀). As the frequency of light (ω) approaches the natural frequency of the electrons (ω₀), the electron's amplitude and phase delay shift drastically. This creates 'normal dispersion', where n increases with frequency (blue light bends more than red).
sections.example: Use a graphical animation of a playground swing: pushing at low frequency vs. pushing at resonance frequency changes how the swing moves.

sections.title: Visualizing Dispersion: The Prism
sections.content: Connect the microscopic physics to macroscopic observation. Because different colors have different indices of refraction in glass, they bend at different angles (Snell's Law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂).
sections.example: Show a classic triangular prism splitting white light into a rainbow, labeling the paths of blue vs. red light clearly.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-world Application
sections.content: Summarize that color dependence is an inevitable consequence of light-matter interaction. Mention Chromatic Aberration in high-end camera lenses as a critical engineering challenge resulting from this principle.
sections.example: An 'Achromatic Doublet' lens system used in a telescope, where two different glass types are combined to cancel out the color-bending effects.
